justification: A tight-aggressive baseline for six-handed fixed-limit hold'em. When nobody has put money in yet we raise or fold; only the small blind sometimes completes, because it is already half in and only the big blind is left. Raising beats limping in limit: a raise sometimes wins the blinds at once, thins the field, and puts more money in while our hand is most likely ahead, and the raiser keeps the lead into the flop. Ranges widen as position improves, because fewer players behind us means fewer chances that someone holds a better hand, and acting last on every later street is worth extra hands. Facing a raise we mostly re-raise or fold; we call only when the price is good or our hand plays well in a bigger field. Played over many hands, the chart aims to put money in voluntarily with about 18 to 26 percent of hands and to raise first with about 14 to 22 percent.

spots.justification: Five players still act behind us, so the chance that one of them holds a better hand is highest here. We open only hands that stay strong when called: pairs down to the middle, every suited ace, the best suited broadways and the top offsuit aces. Weaker offsuit hands are folded because they are easily dominated and we will usually play out of position.

We add the smaller middle pairs, a few more suited connectors and one-gappers, and the next layer of offsuit broadways such as king-jack and queen-jack. Everything we would open from the earlier seat is still a raise here.

spots.justification: Only the button and the two blinds remain, and the blinds will be out of position after the flop. A raise here often takes the blinds without a fight, so we open every pair, more suited kings and connectors, and offsuit aces down to about ace-seven. Hands that rely on hitting a big draw are still mostly left out, because the button can call or re-raise behind us.

Stealing the blinds is now a big part of the profit, so we raise any ace, most kings, connected suited hands and offsuit broadways. We still fold the weakest unconnected offsuit hands, which win too rarely when a blind calls and checks to us.

We raise to isolate the limper with hands that play well heads-up: big pairs, strong aces and suited broadways. Small pairs and suited aces prefer a cheap multiway flop, so they limp along hoping to hit a set or a flush.

Weaker offsuit hands fold because they are often dominated by a re-raising range.
